<reason>PRO won by keeping the motion comparative and forcing CON to defend a zero-effect counterfactual. CON's own phrasing ("changed skylines," "trims prices a few percent") became PRO's evidence, and CON's walk-back to "a ceiling" required the claim that every added unit is filled by someone who otherwise would not have bid on existing stock — PRO named that as a horizontal demand curve and CON never squarely refuted it, only re-asserted that in-migration "restores the pressure." PRO's closing point that the 40% national surge is baseline in both worlds neutralized CON's main weighing move; CON's reply that "a counterfactual leaving rents at today's levels is not cheaper" simply assumes the conclusion. CON fought well: Miami was a real counterexample, the "immunized claim" attack landed rhetorically, and the sprawl-adds-land vs infill-reprices-land distinction was genuinely original. But PRO's Miami answer (glut/bust is supply moving prices; ask what Miami costs with those buyers and no towers) held up, and Minneapolis went unaddressed all debate. PRO's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a minor execution cost that does not offset the substantive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1/B4.7–B5.3 sequence: seizing CON's "trims prices a few percent," reframing it as the comparative motion conceded, then pinning CON's retreat to "roughly unchanged" on an unstated horizontal-demand assumption CON could only answer by assertion.</best_rebuttal>
